title: 2 Samuel 15:24–29
context: Zadok and Abiathar bring the ark of God out of Jerusalem, but David sends it back. He refuses to treat the ark as a good-luck charm and entrusts his future to the LORD: if God favors him, he will return; if not, let God do as seems good. David also arranges for the priests and their sons to send him news from the city.

verses.text: Behold, Zadok also came, and all the Levites with him, bearing the ark of the covenant of God; and they set down God’s ark; and Abiathar went up until all the people finished passing out of the city.
verses.arminianNotes: Zadok, Abiathar, and the Levites bring "the ark of the covenant of God" out of the city. Arminian readers see the priests' loyalty to David and their desire to keep God's presence with the king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the ark represented God's throne among his people (2 Samuel 6:2). Bringing it out raises the question of whether David will try to use God's presence for his own advantage.

verses.text: The king said to Zadok, “Carry God’s ark back into the city. If I find favor in the LORD’s eyes, he will bring me again, and show me both it and his habitation;
verses.arminianNotes: "Carry God's ark back into the city. If I find favor in the LORD's eyes, he will bring me again." Arminian readers see humble trust: David will not presume on God or treat the ark as a lucky charm.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David submitting to God's sovereign will. He knows God's favor cannot be manipulated, and that restoration depends entirely on God's free decision, not on possessing the ark.

verses.text: but if he says, ‘I have no delight in you,’ behold, here I am. Let him do to me as seems good to him.”
verses.arminianNotes: "Here I am. Let him do to me as seems good to him." Arminian readers see a model of surrender: David accepts that God may discipline him and responds with humility rather than resentment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear a confession of trust in God's sovereign goodness. David places his life entirely in God's hands, accepting whatever God decides as right, even if it means losing his throne.

verses.text: The king said also to Zadok the priest, “Aren’t you a seer? Return into the city in peace, and your two sons with you, Ahimaaz your son and Jonathan the son of Abiathar.
verses.arminianNotes: David calls Zadok a seer and sends him back with Ahimaaz and Jonathan. Arminian readers note that trust in God does not exclude wise planning; David acts responsibly while depending on God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God's sovereignty and human means work together. David trusts God's will and also arranges intelligence from the city, using ordinary means God may bless.

verses.text: Behold, I will stay at the fords of the wilderness until word comes from you to inform me.”
verses.arminianNotes: David will wait "at the fords of the wilderness" for word. Arminian readers see a leader who waits patiently, neither rushing ahead nor giving up, but staying ready to act on what he learns.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that David's waiting reflects dependence on God's timing. He does not force events but positions himself to respond as God's providence unfolds through the messengers.

verses.text: Zadok therefore and Abiathar carried God’s ark to Jerusalem again; and they stayed there.
verses.arminianNotes: Zadok and Abiathar carry the ark back to Jerusalem. Arminian readers note the priests' obedience to David's wish and their willingness to stay in danger to serve him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the ark returns to its place, a quiet sign that God's presence is not bound to David's fortunes. God's throne remains secure even while the human king is in flight.
